Require \(52.9 \times \frac{n^{2}}{Z} = 70.53\), i.e. \(\frac{n^{2}}{Z} = 1.333 = \frac{4}{3}\).

Statement I: count the electrons around sulphur. \(SO_{2}\) (\(O=S=O\)) has 10 electrons on S, \(SO_{3}\) has 12, \(SF_{4}\) has 10 and \(SF_{6}\) has 12 — all four are expanded-octet species; only \(H_{2}S\) has a normal octet. So FOUR compounds violate the octet rule, not three. Statement I is FALSE.
Statement II: lone pairs on the central atom — \(H_{2}O\) 2, \(ClF_{3}\) 2, \(SF_{4}\) 1, \(NH_{3}\) 1, \(BrF_{5}\) 1, \(XeF_{4}\) 2.
Set 1 \([H_{2}O, ClF_{3}, SF_{4}]\): 2, 2, 1 — no.
Set 2 \([NH_{3}, BrF_{5}, SF_{4}]\): 1, 1, 1 — YES.
Set 3 \([BrF_{5}, ClF_{3}, XeF_{4}]\): 1, 2, 2 — no.
Set 4 \([XeF_{4}, ClF_{3}, H_{2}O]\): 2, 2, 2 — no.
Exactly one set qualifies, so Statement II is TRUE.

(A) Isothermal REVERSIBLE expansion of an ideal gas: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w = nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\) — matches (II).
(B) FREE expansion: \(p_{ext} = 0\) so \(w = 0\), and isothermally \(\Delta U = 0\), hence \(q = 0\) — matches (I).
(C) IRREVERSIBLE compression against constant external pressure: \(w = -p_{ext}\Delta V\) — matches (III).
(D) CYCLIC reversible process: entropy is a state function, so \(\Delta S = \oint \frac{q_{rev}}{T} = 0\) — matches (IV).
Hence A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

For \(A_{x}B_{y} \rightleftharpoons xA^{y+} + yB^{x-}\) at concentration \(c\) and degree of dissociation \(\alpha\):
\([A^{y+}] = xc\alpha\), \([B^{x-}] = yc\alpha\), \([A_{x}B_{y}] = c(1-\alpha) \approx c\) since the electrolyte is weak and the solution concentrated (\(\alpha \ll 1\)).
\(K = \frac{(xc\alpha)^{x}(yc\alpha)^{y}}{c} = x^{x}y^{y}c^{x+y-1}\alpha^{x+y}\).
Therefore \(\alpha^{x+y} = \frac{K}{c^{x+y-1}x^{x}y^{y}}\) and \(\alpha = \left(\frac{K}{c^{x+y-1}x^{x}y^{y}}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}}\).

The plot is the Nernst equation \(E = E^{\circ} - \frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log Q\) rearranged to \(\frac{E-E^{\circ}}{RT/F} = -\frac{2.303}{n}\log Q\), giving straight lines of slope proportional to \(1/n\), exactly as drawn for \(n = 1, 2, 3\).
(A) is correct: multiplying the anode half-reaction by \(n_{2}\) and the cathode half-reaction by \(n_{1}\) cancels the electrons and gives the stated overall equation.
(B) is correct — the electrons released at the anode are exactly those consumed at the cathode.
(C) is correct — \(n\) in the Nernst equation is the number of electrons transferred.
(D) is INCORRECT: reversible electrical work is the PRODUCT of the charge moved and the potential difference, \(w_{elec} = -nFE\), not their ratio.

Across a period, ionization enthalpy increases left to right, so the element at the extreme LEFT (an alkali metal) has the LOWEST first ionization enthalpy of that period.
Electron gain enthalpy becomes more negative across a period, so the element at the extreme RIGHT excluding noble gases (a halogen) has the HIGHEST magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy.
Hence: lowest and highest.

Statement I: observed bond angles are \(F_{2}O \approx 103.2^{\circ}\), \(H_{2}O = 104.5^{\circ}\), \(Cl_{2}O \approx 110.9^{\circ}\). Highly electronegative F pulls bonding pairs away from O, reducing bond-pair repulsion and closing the angle; the bulky, less electronegative Cl opens it. So \(F_{2}O < H_{2}O < Cl_{2}O\) is TRUE.
Statement II: covalent character in group-14 tetrahalides decreases down the group. \(SiF_{4}\) is a covalent, volatile molecular gas, whereas \(SnF_{4}\) and \(PbF_{4}\) are ionic solids. Since \(SiF_{4}\) is not ionic, Statement II is FALSE.

Configurations: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}\), \(Mn = [Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}\).
First ionization: Cr loses its single \(4s\) electron easily (\(\Delta_{i}H_{1} \approx 653\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)) whereas Mn must break a paired \(4s^{2}\) shell (\(\approx 717\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)). So \(Mn > Cr\) — statement (C) is correct and (A) is wrong.
Second ionization: \(Cr^{+}\) is \([Ar]3d^{5}\), an extra-stable half-filled configuration, so removing a second electron is very difficult (\(\approx 1592\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)); \(Mn^{+}\) is \([Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}\) and simply loses the remaining \(4s\) electron (\(\approx 1509\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)). So \(Cr > Mn\) — statement (B) is correct and (D) is wrong.
Hence B and C only.

In the figure of methyl acetate \(CH_{3}-C(=O)-O-CH_{3}\), \(\alpha\) is the carbonyl \(C=O\), \(\beta\) is the bond from the carbonyl carbon to the ester oxygen, and \(\gamma\) is the \(O-CH_{3}\) bond.
\(\alpha\) is a full double bond, the shortest (\(\approx 120\) pm).
\(\beta\) is a single bond but acquires partial double-bond character from the resonance donation of the ester oxygen lone pair into the carbonyl, so it is shortened (\(\approx 134\) pm).
\(\gamma\) is a pure \(sp^{3}\) \(C-O\) single bond with no such shortening, the longest (\(\approx 144\) pm).
Hence \(\alpha < \beta < \gamma\).

An OPTICALLY ACTIVE \(C_{4}H_{9}Br\) must be 2-bromobutane (the only chiral isomer).
With alcoholic KOH it eliminates to the Saytzeff product but-2-ene, [A].
\(Br_{2}\) adds to give 2,3-dibromobutane, [B].
Double dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH followed by sodamide gives but-2-yne, [C].

[D] is a METHYL ketone, so it responds to the haloform (iodoform) test, giving yellow \(CHI_{3}\). Lucas test is for alcohols; silver mirror (Tollens) and Benedict tests are for aldehydes and reducing sugars, and a ketone gives neither.

The figure shows benzyl phenyl ether, \(C_{6}H_{5}-O-CH_{2}-C_{6}H_{5}\), treated with HI.
In an alkyl aryl ether the \(O\) lone pair is delocalised into the ring, giving the \(O-Ar\) bond partial double-bond character; that bond is NOT broken. Cleavage occurs at the \(O-CH_{2}\) bond, and here the benzylic carbon further favours attack by \(I^{-}\).
Products are therefore PHENOL and BENZYL IODIDE, not benzyl alcohol and an iodo-aromatic compound. Statement I is FALSE.

From the figure the substrate is propanoic acid, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH\).
(i) \(NH_{3}/\Delta\) converts it to the ammonium salt and then to propanamide, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CONH_{2}\).
(ii) \(NaOH/Br_{2}\) is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which removes one carbon to give ethanamine, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}\).
(iii) \(HNO_{2}/H_{2}O\) at \(0^{\circ}C\) on a primary ALIPHATIC amine gives an unstable diazonium ion that immediately loses \(N_{2}\), yielding ethanol.
(iv) Benzenediazonium chloride warmed with ethanol is REDUCED: the ethanol acts as the hydride donor, being oxidised to ethanal, and the aryl group is replaced by hydrogen with loss of \(N_{2}\).
Hence X is benzene.

\(Br_{2}/KOH\) (alcoholic) is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which requires an UNSUBSTITUTED amide \(RCONH_{2}\) and gives the primary amine \(RNH_{2}\) with loss of one carbon.
The six compounds are: \(C_{6}H_{5}CONH_{2}\), \(C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}CONH_{2}\), \(CH_{3}CONH_{2}\), \(C_{6}H_{11}CONHC_{2}H_{5}\), \((CH_{3})_{3}CCONHCH_{3}\) and \(C_{6}H_{11}CONH_{2}\).
The two N-substituted amides (the N-ethyl cyclohexanecarboxamide and the N-methyl pivalamide) have no \(-NH_{2}\) and cannot undergo the reaction at all, so four remain:
\(C_{6}H_{5}CONH_{2} \rightarrow\) aniline; \(C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}CONH_{2} \rightarrow\) benzylamine; \(CH_{3}CONH_{2} \rightarrow\) methylamine; \(C_{6}H_{11}CONH_{2} \rightarrow\) cyclohexylamine.
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis proceeds by \(S_{N}2\) attack of the phthalimide anion on a halide, so it CANNOT make aromatic amines — aniline is ruled out. Benzylamine, methylamine and cyclohexylamine are all accessible from the corresponding halides.
Hence 3 compounds satisfy both requirements.

From the figure the substrate is glucose, \(CHO-(CHOH)_{4}-CH_{2}OH\).
(i) Prolonged heating with HI reduces every oxygenated carbon, giving n-hexane.
(ii) n-Hexane over \(V_{2}O_{5}\) at 773 K and 10-20 atm undergoes aromatisation (cyclisation with loss of \(4H_{2}\)) to benzene.
(iii) Benzoyl chloride with anhydrous \(AlCl_{3}\) acylates benzene (Friedel-Crafts acylation) to give benzophenone, \((C_{6}H_{5})_{2}C=O\), which is X.
Counting in benzophenone: each ring contributes 3 \(\pi\) bonds, so \(2 \times 3 = 6\) ring \(\pi\) bonds plus the carbonyl \(\pi\) bond \(= 7\) \(\pi\) bonds \(= 14\) \(\pi\) electrons. The carbonyl oxygen carries 2 lone pairs \(= 4\) electrons.
Total \(= 14 + 4 = 18\) electrons.

This is the classical brown-ring test for nitrate. Freshly prepared \(FeSO_{4}\) reduces the nitrate and the nitric oxide so produced is captured by \(Fe^{2+}\):
\(NO + [Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+} \rightarrow [Fe(H_{2}O)_{5}(NO)]^{2+} + H_{2}O\).
The brown ring is the nitrosyl complex, written simply as \([Fe(NO)]SO_{4}\), in which iron is formally \(Fe(I)\) and the ligand is \(NO^{+}\).
